Them: That lives on the customer record, not the item. Each customer has a minimum remaining shelf life in days, and picking skips any lot that is too close to expiry for that customer.
Me: Fennimore needs 150 days and Hollowbrook Unified needs 120. I'll send you the minimums for all 58 customers by Friday, March 26.
Them: 58 customers with 310 ship-to addresses is manageable. Quenby sends the addresses through the integration, so we only need the shelf life rules from you.
Them: Now locations. How many bin locations does each site have?
Me: 1,850 at Dayton, 620 at Toledo and 940 at Fort Wayne, so 3,410 in all.
Them: For each location we need the site, aisle, bay, level and position, the storage class and the pallet capacity. We'll give you a template at the kickoff, and we need the Dayton file by Friday, April 9.
Me: Our Dayton locations are named like D-04-12-B, which is aisle 4, bay 12, level B. Can you keep our names?
Them: Yes, we keep your names exactly and generate a barcode for each one. We print the 1,850 Dayton labels at our office and ship them to you by Friday, May 28.
Me: And my team puts them on the racks?
Them: Yes, between Monday, May 31 and Friday, June 4. Two people with a lift can usually do it in three days.
Them: Opening stock next. We don't take your ERP balances, because they are rarely accurate down to the lot. Instead you count everything at cutover and we load the count.
Me: A full count at Dayton on Saturday, June 12. We usually hold about 5,200 pallets, and with 20 counters that is about 260 pallets each, so one morning is enough.
Them: Start at 6 a.m. Each pallet scan records the location, the SKU, the lot code and the expiry date, and a pallet with an unreadable label gets a new label printed on the spot.
Me: Our lot code is the plant letter, a two-digit year, the day of the year and the line number, like D-27-041-2.
Them: Tallyhouse reads that format, so it works out the production date and then the expiry from the shelf life. Is the shelf life the same for all items?
Me: Most are 12 months, but the four dairy-based sauce families have nine months.
Them: That sits on the item record, so it's no problem. Open orders last: at cutover Quenby sends the orders due to ship from Monday to Wednesday, about 600 lines, and we load them through the integration on Sunday morning.
Me: How do we judge the mock loads?
Them: We measure the share of records that load without errors. We want 95 percent in the first mock on April 12, 98 percent in the second on April 30, and 99.5 percent in the dress rehearsal on May 7.
Me: What if the dress rehearsal misses the bar?
Them: Then we run another one before acceptance testing starts on May 17, and that rerun is at our cost.
Me: And what about new products created in the weeks before go-live?
Them: We freeze the item master on Friday, June 4. Any new SKU after that needs Walt's approval and is entered by hand.
Them: The go or no-go decision is on Sunday, June 13 at 4 p.m., with Walt, you and me. If it's no-go, you stay on the old process and we agree a new date.

Them: You keep paper pick lists printed from Quenby for the first two weeks as a fallback, and Quenby stays the system of record for orders during that period.
Me: Good, I'll tell Walt. Two weeks of paper fallback after June 14.
Them: Raul here, I lead training. Our approach is to train the trainers first, and then let them train their own people with our help. How many trainers do you want on your side?

Them: No, they have their own one-day courses: Toledo on Tuesday, July 13 and Fort Wayne on Tuesday, September 7.
Me: What do the super-users learn on those days?
Them: Everything an end user does, plus how to fix the common problems, such as a rejected scan, a wrong lot, a pallet in the wrong location, or a printer that stops. They also get practice scripts for the sandbox, which opens on April 19.
Me: Dayton's 96 end users are the next step. How do you propose to run it?
Them: Groups of eight, 90 minutes each, which makes 12 sessions, three a day from Monday, June 7 to Thursday, June 10. The sessions start at 7 a.m., 1:30 p.m. and 6 p.m., so every shift has a slot.
Me: Walt will ask about floor coverage. Ninety-six people leaving the floor for 90 minutes is a lot, although with eight at a time it should be manageable.
Them: That's why we keep the groups at eight. Walt chooses who goes in which group so that every line keeps enough people, and the super-users help to run each session.
Me: About 16 of our Dayton staff prefer Spanish. Can you teach in Spanish?
Them: Yes. Rosa, one of our trainers, teaches in Spanish. Two of the 12 sessions will be in Spanish, with eight people each, and that is included in the fixed fee.
Me: Great. What about reference material on the floor?
Them: Laminated quick-reference cards, English on one side and Spanish on the other. We print 150 for Dayton, 60 for Toledo and 80 for Fort Wayne.
Me: What do the cards cover?
Them: Six tasks: receive, putaway, pick, pack, move and count. Those are the six that every end user does, and they are also what we test at the end of the session.
Me: How do you test them?
Them: Everyone completes a practical check on a handheld, doing all six tasks, and they pass with five out of six. Logins are only issued after the check.
Me: And if someone fails?
Them: They get a 30-minute retake with a super-user the next day. If they still fail, they come to another session with us, and that stays inside the included training days.
Me: How many training days are included in the fixed fee?
Them: 20 trainer days across the three sites. Any extra day is $1,650, as Hollis said earlier.
Me: The supervisors need something different. They have to read the dashboards and approve stock adjustments.

Them: There's a two-day admin course, remote, four hours each day, on Monday, May 3 and Tuesday, May 4. After that those three can change locations, users and printers themselves.
Me: Toledo has 38 end users and Fort Wayne has 52. How do their sessions work?
Them: Toledo needs five sessions, from Monday, July 19 to Wednesday, July 21. Fort Wayne needs seven sessions, on Wednesday, September 8, Thursday, September 9 and Friday, September 10, which is the week before Beck's count.
Me: Good, that keeps clear of the count. Do you also provide videos?

Them: Ingrid here, I manage support. Let me start with hours. Our standard support runs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday, and severity 1 problems are covered around the clock.
Me: That doesn't match how we operate. All three sites run Monday to Saturday, Dayton's early shift starts at 4:30 a.m., and the late shift ends at 11 p.m.

Them: That is more than our standard, but for a customer with three sites I can do it. Severity 1 around the clock, and severity 2 and 3 from 4:30 a.m. to 11:30 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Saturday, with no extra charge.
Me: Thank you. How do you define the severity levels?
Them: Severity 1 means a site can't receive or ship. Severity 2 means a major function is degraded but there is a workaround. Severity 3 is a minor problem, and severity 4 is a question or a request.
Me: And the response times for each?
Them: For severity 1 we respond within 30 minutes, update you every hour, and aim to restore service within four hours. For severity 2 we respond within two hours and give a fix or workaround within one business day.
Them: Severity 3 gets a response by the next business day and a fix in the next release or within 10 business days. Severity 4 gets an answer within three business days.
Me: How do my people reach you at 4:30 in the morning?
Them: There is a dedicated phone line and a ticket portal. The phone is for severity 1 and 2 and the portal for everything else. Callum is your named support engineer, and he has a backup on the phone rota.
Me: Our first line is the super-users, so they will only call you for what they can't fix themselves.
Them: That is the model we recommend. We'll agree a short checklist with them so that every ticket arrives with the site, the device, the user and the time.
Me: Now uptime. What do you commit to?
Them: 99.9 percent per month, measured outside the Sunday maintenance window from 2 a.m. to 5 a.m. Eastern.
Me: And what do we get if you miss it?
Them: Service credits on that month's fees: 5 percent if uptime is below 99.9 percent, 10 percent if it is below 99.5, and 20 percent if it is below 98.
Me: I'd like the credits to apply automatically, without me having to make a claim.
Them: We can do that. The credit appears on the next invoice, and the monthly uptime figure is in the report you receive.
Me: Now hypercare. What happens on June 14?

Me: And the response times during hypercare?
Them: We halve them. Severity 1 gets a response within 15 minutes, and severity 2 within one hour.
Me: What about Toledo and Fort Wayne?
Them: At Toledo, Marcus is on site for three days, July 26 to 28, with remote support until Friday, August 13. At Fort Wayne both consultants are on site for five days from September 20, and then remote until October 8.

Me: Tell me how cycle counting works in Tallyhouse.
Them: Items are in three classes. A items are counted monthly, B items quarterly and C items twice a year. The system creates the count tasks every morning, about 80 locations a day at Dayton.

Them: A supervisor approves any difference above two cases or $200, and every adjustment is logged with the user, the device and the time.
Me: For Toledo, temperature is the most important alert we have.

Them: Sunita here, I'm the security officer at Brennivale, so let me cover where your data lives and how we protect it. Tallyhouse runs in the cloud, with a primary region in Ohio and a secondary region in Virginia.
Me: Nadia asked me about backups and recovery. What are the numbers?
Them: We back up every four hours and keep the backups for 35 days. If the primary region fails, we restore in the secondary region within eight hours, and we test that recovery once a year and share the results with you.
Me: So we could lose at most four hours of data, and be down for at most eight hours. Is that a commitment or a target?
Them: It's a commitment, and it will be written into the agreement as at most four hours of data and at most eight hours to restore.
Me: What about encryption?
Them: AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher for data in transit, including between the handhelds and our servers.
Me: How do people log in? Many of our floor staff don't have a company email address.
Them: Supervisors and administrators sign in through single sign-on with your company directory, and administrators also need multi-factor authentication. Floor staff scan their badge and enter a four-digit PIN on the handheld.
Me: That works for us. How are permissions handled?
Them: There are seven standard roles: receiver, putaway driver, picker, shipper, inventory controller, supervisor and administrator. Your administrators can create more, and every action is logged with the user and the time.
Me: How long do you keep those logs?
Them: The audit log stays online for 13 months, and the transaction history for seven years, as Tomas said earlier.
Me: Does anyone at Brennivale see our data?
Them: Only support staff, and only when a ticket requires it. Each access is logged, and you can ask us for the access log at any time.

Them: Yes, once a year with 30 days' notice, at your cost, and we answer their findings in writing within 30 days. You also receive our SOC 2 Type II report every year under an NDA, with a summary of our independent penetration test.
